headline: Boston schools preview bell-to-bell ban on students’ personal devices
dek: The proposed Pre-K–12 policy would keep phones, smartwatches, personal laptops and other devices secured throughout the school day starting in 2027, but the School Committee still must vote.
body: Boston Public Schools is preparing a districtwide policy that would require students to keep personal electronic devices turned off, secured and inaccessible for the entire school day, including class changes, lunch and recess. The proposal was previewed in a [Boston Public Schools memorandum](https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1791900078/bostonpublicschoolsorg/oaaavqubbimurzqmiq14/BPSDraftMemoCellPhonePolicy.pdf) dated Oct. 14 and posted with that evening’s [School Committee materials](https://www.bostonpublicschools.org/school-committee/school-committee-meetings/~board/2026/post/october-14-2026-presentations-and-materials). The formal policy is expected to come before the committee for action in January 2027, so the plan is not yet a rule.

The draft would go beyond a cellphone-only restriction. It lists smartwatches, tablets, personal laptops, Bluetooth devices and artificial-intelligence glasses among the equipment students could not possess during the school day. Personal laptops and tablets would not be permitted at school under the proposal; BPS says school-administered devices would be supplied when needed for learning. The district says the policy would replace its current electronics policy, which the memo identifies as dating to 2005.

The proposed scope covers every BPS student from prekindergarten through Grade 12. Exceptions would be available when an Individualized Education Program team determines that a device is a necessary and reasonable accommodation for a student’s education, with medical documentation considered when appropriate. The draft therefore treats access needs as part of the policy design, rather than leaving families to seek an informal exemption after enforcement begins.

How schools would secure the devices remains unsettled. The memo gives individual school leaders discretion to choose methods such as locking pouches, lockers or dedicated storage, while the central office would provide technical assistance, progress-monitoring tools and restorative curriculum resources. BPS also says it is researching grant opportunities that could help pay for implementation. The district has not yet published a single enforcement model or a final estimate of what storage, staffing and replacement costs would be for schools and families.

The proposal follows a round of district engagement that BPS says included three youth focus groups involving Sociedad Latina, the Boston Student Advisory Council and English High School students. The district also held a parent focus group with St. Stephen’s and an educator focus group at English High, surveyed school leaders and administrators, and convened a four-session working group of community advocates, educators, parents and students. The memo says the administrator survey drew 92 responses. Those figures describe the process BPS says it used; they do not establish that the wider school community has reached a consensus.

BPS says the policy is based on research about the effects of constant screen exposure and social media on adolescent mental health and focus, and that its goals are improved well-being, academic engagement and school culture. The district’s memo cites the American Academy of Pediatrics but does not present local before-and-after results because the districtwide rule has not been implemented. Research cited by the [Boston Globe](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/10/14/metro/boston-school-cellphone-ban/) has found mixed academic effects from cellphone restrictions, making the district’s future progress measures important to evaluating whether the policy achieves its stated aims.

The Boston proposal also lands in the middle of a broader Massachusetts debate. The Globe reported that a statewide cellphone measure remains stalled while the Legislature has debated restrictions on youth social-media use. Boston’s City Council adopted a 2025 resolution supporting a districtwide bell-to-bell policy, but that resolution did not itself impose rules on BPS. Some Boston schools already use phone pouches or require devices to remain out of sight, according to Superintendent Mary Skipper’s comments reported by the Globe; the new proposal would make a version of the restriction common across the district and extend it to more devices.

The next phase is policy development rather than immediate enforcement. BPS says it will continue listening sessions with students, families and educators, refine its progress metrics, and issue implementation guidance before submitting the final policy and planning for budget needs. [WHDH reported](https://whdh.com/news/boston-public-schools-proposes-ban-of-electronic-devices-for-students/) that the committee has not yet settled how violations would be handled and that a formal proposal is expected in January. If the committee approves it, BPS intends the policy to be in place on the first day of the 2027–2028 school year, giving schools months to choose storage systems and explain the changes to families.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Boston Public Schools previews 2027 bell-to-bell device ban
seoDescription: Boston Public Schools is preparing a Pre-K–12 policy that would secure students’ personal devices throughout the school day starting in 2027.
